source.title: RITA: a Study on Scaling Up Generative Protein Sequence Models
source.authors: Daniel Hesslow; Niccoló Zanichelli; Pascal Notin; Iacopo Poli; D. Marks

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in protein sequence models and reports departures from a single power-law pattern, refining the scope of scaling-law claims.
record.gate_note: The authors report perplexity across model sizes and datasets, a loss-versus-compute scaling result, and downstream metrics across model sizes. Results cited from other papers are not included. The prompt-tuning comparison is not treated as a scaling-law result because it reports a tuned-versus-base comparison rather than a fitted scaling relationship.
record.test_reason: The study trains four autoregressive protein-sequence transformers (to 1.2B parameters) and fits loss against compute. It reports an exponent of 0.74 and some deviation from a power law, and gives downstream metrics by model size. This is a new setting (protein sequences) with results on V5, V6 and V7. It is T3 rather than T5: the study does not argue that a version is wrong.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors present RITA as a first step toward protein scaling laws and report benefits from scale on perplexity, fitness and enzyme-function prediction. They report a compute-scaling exponent of 0.74, steeper than NLP's ~0.5, with some deviation from a power law. All but the smallest model still appear undertrained despite training far beyond the NLP-optimal token count.
record.recipe_differences: Studies autoregressive protein sequence models rather than natural-language models, with four model sizes, protein datasets, and downstream protein tasks; it does not reproduce the original natural-language scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that loss scaling departs from a power law, including a sharp decrease for the largest model after substantial training. Their positional-embedding ablation reports different perplexity for RoPE and ALiBi, but this is not a scaling-law comparison.

fits_no_version.finding: The models were trained on 150B amino acids, beyond the ~25B NLP-optimal estimate for XL, yet all but the smallest still appear undertrained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal token-to-parameter ratios estimated for text do not transfer to protein sequence models; protein models are optimally trained on more data.

record.problems: The scaling sweep spans only four models and an order of magnitude in size. The paper reports deviations from the power-law pattern and says larger-scale positional-embedding ablation is needed for reliable results. No uncertainty estimates are given for the reported scaling or downstream results. Table 1 values for the XLarge column conflict with the stated trend and Appendix Table 9.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. The individual ProteinGym assay results in Appendix Tables 5 and 6 are not separately cataloged; only the paper's reported aggregate averages are recorded.

untested.parts: Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer. Protein sequences are the only new modality tested, with only four model sizes.
Whether downstream performance is predicted by pretraining loss. No downstream scaling fit or extrapolation is made.
Parameter counting, training schedule and fitting-method comparisons.
Not tested: natural-language pretraining loss is not measured.
Not tested: there is no fit-then-extrapolate experiment.
Not tested: there is no fixed-compute allocation sweep.
Not tested: there is no shape ablation at fixed parameter count.

missing.what: The fitted scaling law itself: the loss-vs-compute curves for the four models, the fitted form, and the range in PF-days. Only the exponent is captured in r33.
The observation that models trained to 150B amino acids are still undertrained, compared with the 25B optimum estimated from NLP laws.

record.verdict_notes: The flattened text misaligned the columns of Tables 1 and 2. Table 1's apparent 'XL' values are ProtGPT2 baselines, and Table 2's L/XL values are swapped relative to Table 5. The reader's 'challenges' label for V7 was wrong: a deviation from a single power law is what V7 describes, so it supports V7. The evidence is thin: only four model sizes, about one order of magnitude in size, and no uncertainty estimates.

versions.untested_parts: The study examines protein sequence models, not held-out pretraining loss in natural-language models as specified by this version.
It does not fit laws on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not sweep parameter and token allocations under fixed compute or estimate compute-optimal allocations. The optimality estimates it mentions are attributed to other work.
It does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Tests protein-sequence modeling, but not image or video models, repeated-data training, or whether the same fitted power law holds under fine-tuning and transfer.
Reports downstream task metrics by model size, but does not test whether downstream performance is predicted from pretraining loss.
Reports deviations in the protein-model loss curve, but does not compare parameter-counting conventions, fitting methods, or compute-optimal allocations across setups.

rows.subject: RITA models
rows.size_stated: four models spanning up to 1.2 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Measured protein modeling loss as a function of compute.
rows.measure: Protein modeling loss versus compute; reported scaling exponent and curve shape
rows.value: Exponent 0.74; authors report some deviation from a power law, including a sharp loss decrease for the largest model after substantial training.
rows.note: The authors describe a scaling law similar to NLP results, but say the curve deviates from a power law. They also note that loss does not go above 2.8 due to the small vocabulary.
rows.check: For V5 the state is partial: there is a power-law-like fit (exponent 0.74 versus compute), but with stated deviation, including a sharp late loss drop for XL. For V7 the state should be observed: the curve bends away from a single power law and the exponent differs from NLP (~0.5).

relationships.condition: RITA protein LMs, loss vs compute, Small to XL (about 1 order of magnitude in size)
relationships.reason: The authors fit a Kaplan-like scaling law with exponent 0.74 (r33), and per-byte perplexity falls monotonically with size on all four datasets (r17-r32).
relationships.display_finding: A Kaplan-like law fit compute scaling with exponent 0.74, while per-byte perplexity decreased monotonically with size across all four datasets.

relationships.condition: Protein loss curve, especially the largest model late in training
relationships.reason: The authors note deviation from the power law, including a sharp late loss drop for XL and a loss floor set by the small vocabulary (r33).
relationships.display_finding: Loss deviated from the power law, including a sharp late decrease for XL and a floor attributed to the small vocabulary.

relationships.reason: The exponent (0.74) differs markedly from NLP's (~0.5), and the curve deviates from a single power law (r33).
relationships.display_finding: The protein-domain exponent is 0.74 versus approximately 0.5 for NLP, and the compute-loss curve departs from a single power law.

relationships.condition: SwissProt enzyme function (top-1, top-10) and ProteinGym substitution averages
relationships.reason: Accuracy and Spearman correlation rise monotonically with size: r42-r45, r50-r53, and r34-r37 after correction to Table 5.
relationships.display_finding: Enzyme function top-1 and top-10 accuracy and average ProteinGym substitution Spearman correlation increased monotonically with model size.

relationships.condition: ProteinGym indel benchmark (7 assays) and SwissProt top-3
relationships.reason: Medium (0.426) beats Large (0.414) and XL (0.406) on indels (r39-r41); Medium top-3 (90.2) is below Small (90.7) (r46, r47).
relationships.display_finding: Medium scored 0.426 on indels versus Large's 0.414 and XL's 0.406, while its SwissProt top-3 score was 90.2 versus Small's 90.7.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: RITA protein sequence models, up to 1.2 billion parameters
reader_labels.reason: The authors report a scaling exponent of 0.74 and a similar scaling relationship, but also describe deviations from a power law, including a sharp loss decrease for the largest model; see r33.

reader_labels.reason: The authors explicitly report deviations from the power-law curve and a sharp decrease in loss for the largest model; see r33.

reader_labels.reason: Top-1 and top-10 accuracy rise across the reported model sizes, and the authors describe performance as scaling smoothly; see r42-r45 and r50-r53.
